The high replacement cost of these engines 4 makes retrofit solutions the most practical option for near-term methane leak reduction. Hydrogen addition to natural-gas fuel is known to increase flame speed, improve combustion stability, and reduce methane slip; however, large-scale hydrogen blending requires distribution infrastructure that is not yet economically viable. On-demand generation of hydrogen and reactive hydrocarbon species directly within the engine’s fuel line offers a lower-cost alternative. Plasma- based methane reforming enables in-situ fuel additive generation through non-thermal chemical reactions that partially decompose CH into hydrogen (H ) and short-chain hydrocarbons (C H ). 4 2 x y These reactive additives enhance oxidation completeness without altering the base engine configuration. The present project, performed by SwRI with support from Starfire Industries and Cooper Machinery Services, was undertaken to demonstrate a compact plasma reformer capable of providing these benefits to large-bore natural-gas engines. Figure 1. System overview of the plasma fuel reformer integrated with a natural-gas (NG) engine. The power-electronics control module supplies pulsed electrical energy to the plasma reformer, where a portion of the methane (CH ) in the fuel stream is converted into hydrogen (H ) and short-chain hydrocarbons 4 2 (C H ). The reformed fuel is delivered to the NG engine to improve combustion efficiency and reduce x y methane leaks. Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 2 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report 2.2 Project Objectives The overarching technical objective was to reduce methane leaks from large-bore natural-gas engines by 20‒60 percent through partial fuel reforming while maintaining total auxiliary power consumption below one percent of engine output. Specific supporting objectives were to: 1. Design and fabricate a plasma reformer rated for up to 4 kW peak electrical input and 25 – 30 psig operating pressure. 2. Develop and validate a pulsed-power electronics module capable of stable plasma ignition across a range of gas flow conditions. 3. Demonstrate methane-to-hydrogen conversion at the bench scale and in a high-flow test facility (SwRI’s Metering Research Facility or MRF). 4. Integrate and evaluate the reformer on representative natural-gas engines to quantify leak reduction and operability. 5. Assess scalability and commercialization potential for retrofitting existing midstream compression equipment. 2.3 Methodological Approach 2.3.1 Project Structure The project was organized into four technical phases, each with defined milestones and verification criteria: 1. Phase I – Concept Design and Modeling: CFD analyses defined flow distribution, pressure drop, and plasma-zone geometry. Electrical requirements were determined, and system safety specifications were established. 2. Phase II – Bench-Scale Development: The plasma reformer and power-electronics subsystems were fabricated and tested under controlled flow conditions to verify plasma ignition, stability, and hydrogen generation. 3. Phase III – High-Flow Validation: Full-scale operation was demonstrated at SwRI’s MRF to identify limits of plasma stability under realistic gas velocities and pressures. 4.
